reason: *h₁nómn̥ + *dʰeh₁- with the dative (West ch. 10, Schmitt). All four loci checked: Eznik II.3 §24 dnēr nma anun (DMHP), Vuk 'Nahod Simeun' l. 16 lijepo mu ime nađenuo, Od. 19.403-404 ὄνομ' ... θῆαι παιδὶ (AGDT), AVŚ 3.13.3 vār nāma vo hitam (DCS). Object exact in Arm/Gk/Ved. The head verb is shared at root level only: the cells are an Armenian imperfect of the nasal present, a Slavic -nǫ- perfective, a Greek middle root-aorist subjunctive and a Vedic -tá- participle. Only the Greek has the engine's root-aorist stem, and there it is middle and subjunctive. Late or derivative: the Vuk song is a 19th-c. record and its naming is a baptism (pokrsti ga); Eznik is 5th-c. Christian polemic reporting Zurvanite myth. Builder: the Greek root match runs through pie-lex-dheh1ts (θής 'serf'), a wrong-lexeme path. Same formula as fame-013 (eval group).

West's polyptoton 'brother to brother', all three loci checked: Slovo 77 рекоста бо братъ брату (TOROT spi, nom. + dat.), Vǫlundarkviða 23 bróðir á bróður (FJ 1926), MBh 3.158 bhrātā bhrātaram ... abhyabhāṣata (DCS). *bʰréh₂tēr is exact in all three. But the core is one kin noun in a figure that is cross-linguistically commonplace (West lists friend to friend, man to man). The dative follows the Old Russian only (ON á + acc., Skt acc.). The clause head 'said' is interpolated and non-cognate in all three passages. Two of the three witnesses are late or doubtful (Slovo, authenticity debated; MBh, post-Vedic, and not West's own MBh locus). The interpolated wéwket has no labiovelar, against Gk εἶπον (π < *kʷ) and the lexicon's own Proto-Hellenic *weikʷon; no verdict effect, since the verb is interpolated.

Loci checked: RV 3.25.1 diváḥ sūnúr asi, Il. 16.522 Σαρπηδὼν Διὸς υἱός (AGDT), and Rhesa no. 48 Diewo Sunelei (local OCR; this file is Kurschat's revised edition). The genitive *diwés is exact in Ved/Gk. Lith. Dievo is *deywós, a different lexeme. The head *suHnús is exact in Vedic only. Lith. sūnẽlis is a diminutive. Gk υἱός is *suH-iu- (Beekes EDG s.v.: same root, different suffix), so the builder's exact match for υἱός is a false positive and secure_share 0.667 overstates the line. The referents differ (Agni, Sarpedon, the Baltic twins), and 'son of Zeus' is a plain patronymic in Homer. The scholarly claim (West ch. 4) is the motif of the Sons of Sky, which in Vedic is worded divó nápātā, not sūnú-. The copula comes from the Vedic asi, the only branch with a predication. Head root-level outside Vedic, so weak.

West ch. 2 reconstructs the wording *wekʷesh₁ ... *wergoh₁. All parallel loci checked: Il. 1.504 ἢ ἔπει ἢ ἔργῳ, Hymn. Hom. 2.117 (glaux), Beowulf 1100 wordum ne worcum (Grein, so the manuscript reading) and 1834 wordum and worcum, Y. 31.22b vacaŋhā š́iiaōϑanācā (CAB). Each member is exact in only one other branch: *wékʷos in Gk/Av, *wérǵom in Gk/OE. Only Greek has the pair, and the other members are non-cognate (OE word, Av. š́iiaoϑna-). 'Word and deed' is a near-universal merism, and in OE it is mostly Christian (Grein's other instances are religious verse, e.g. Christ and Satan; cf. Lat. uerbo et opere). The note answers this honestly by citing only the secular Beowulf passages. The instrumental and the -kʷe are well chosen (Av. vacaŋhā ... -cā).

West ch. 2: 'come to one's mother's knees' = be born, Greek and Norse only. Hes. Th. 460 μητρὸς πρὸς γούναθ' ἵκοιτο (glaux, checked) and Sigurðarkviða in skamma (FJ 1926 st. 46 and Neckel/TITUS st. 45, both checked) fyr kné móður. Both nouns are exact (γόνυ = kné, μήτηρ = móðir), so head and modifier are shared at formation level. The idiom is specific, and both contexts are birth. The verb is renewed (ἱκνέομαι / koma) and correctly left out. The bare goal accusative replaces the two different prepositions; as an np fragment it is an engine convention, not attested, but it is honestly explained. GEN méh₂tr̥s matches ON móður (and Ved. mātúr). The plural follows Greek.

The core, the dative *diwéy ph₂tréy, is exact and well documented (Schmitt §288, West ch. 4). Il. 17.498 and Od. 13.51 εὐξάμενος/-οι Διὶ πατρί, Il. 24.287-288 (AGDT) and Tab. Ig. IIb 22-23, 26 Iuvepatre (Buck OCR) are all checked. But the clause head is not shared. In Umbrian the dative depends on sestu / fetu, and vufru is an adjective of the calf ('votive'), not a verb of vowing. Gk εὔχομαι is an e-grade thematic middle. The engine's o-grade causative *h₁wogʷʰéye- is Latin voveō, which stands only in the support ref Cato Agr. 83.1, so P2 leaks into the output. The plan lists it in `secure` although the builder gives level none. Cato Agr. 134.1 (LASLA: Iano Ioui Iunoni praefato) has *dyēws only.

The NP is a recognised equation: priyáṃ nā́ma = OE frēo-nama (Scheller; Schmitt §§97, 373; West ch. 10). RV 10.84.5c, 10.123.7d, 7.56.10a (VedaWeb) and Crist 636 freónoman cende (Grein; Exeter Book, no apparatus note) are checked. Both members are exact, though OE has a compound and Vedic a syntagm. But the frame is stitched: the verb comes from RV 10.123.7, whose object is the plural priyā́ṇi, while the singular comes from 10.84.5 (with gr̥ṇīmasi). In Crist 636 the subject is Job and the object is Christ, so cende is 'declared, proclaimed' (cennan II), not 'begot': the English 'He begot a dear name' fits neither text. The OE witness is a Christian poem, and the word itself means 'surname' (Bede). Schmitt calls the pair an idiom, 'not poetic phraseology'. Cut it to the NP and it would be sound.

The only word shared is the commonest verb of knowing, in passages that are not parallel. AVŚ 1.32.1 idaṃ janāsaḥ vidatha (DCS: 2pl, Tense=Past) is an incipit exhortation. Vǫluspá vituð ér enn, eða hvat? (FJ 1926 st. 26, 32 ff.; Neckel st. 27, 28, 33 ...) is a mid-poem refrain question with a pronoun and no vocative. The verb equation is the author's own; Specht's and Schmitt's claim concerns hljóð : śru- and kind : jána- in Vǫluspá 1, which this line does not use. The vocative comes from Vǫluspá 1, where kindir is the accusative object of biðja, a different stanza (stitched), and it is root-level only (jána- *ǵónh₁o- vs kind *ǵn̥h₁tí-). 'It' is Vedic only. Builder: ON vita reaches *wóyde through non:vissa → *widtós, a wrong-lexeme evidence path.

*ḱred dʰeh₁- + dative of the one trusted (Schmitt §§445-449, de Vaan s.v. crēdō): an accepted lexical equation, exact as a compound in three branches. All checked: RV 2.12.5 śrát asmai dhatta (VedaWeb), Plaut. Epid. 340 crede modo mihi (LASLA), Wb. 18c11 ni cretid dó (Doyle). All three are present-system forms with zero-grade *dʰh₁- before the ending. The stem types differ (Vedic reduplicated, Latin/Celtic thematized), and the note states this honestly; this differs from a tense or aspect mismatch. The dative pronouns are non-cognate, honestly interpolated. Caveats: the Irish is a negated indicative in a gloss on Gal. 1.8 (Christian, possibly shaped by Latin credere + dat.), and Plautus adapts Greek comedy, though that matters for calqued collocations, not for a native verb's valency. The Vedic and the Latin alone carry the line. The Vedic tmesis is not modelled.

RV 1.94.13 deváḥ devā́nām asi (VedaWeb; the formula recurs in 1.31.1, 10.150.4 ...) and Carmen Saliare diuom deo (Baehrens FPR, checked with its apparatus: Flor. diuum, supplicante corrected by Grotefend). *deywós is exact as both head and genitive in both branches, and West ch. 2 makes the comparison. But the elative 'god of gods' is a widespread figure that is productive in Vedic (vásur vásūnām in the same stanza). The Latin is one fragmentary, partly unintelligible Saturnian line, known only through Varro, with the noun in the dative and no predication. The copula and the 2sg come from the Vedic only.

RV 10.65.15 devā́n ... amŕ̥tān vavande (VedaWeb) and Plaut. Amph. 1093 inuocat deos inmortalis (LASLA), both checked. *deywós is exact; 'immortal' is root-level only (Lat. in-mortālis is a new formation, as West says). The verb ǵʰuHéyeti stands in neither passage (vand- vs inuocāre), so the frame is larger than the core. The pairing is near-universal (P5), and Plautus is adapting a Greek original (Amphitruo), so di immortales there probably renders ἀθάνατοι θεοί. Honestly graded weak by its author.

At the reject edge. RV 3.2.7 svàr mahát and Hes. Th. 19 Ἠέλιόν τε μέγαν are both checked; Hesiod is in glaux, so the note's 'not in local corpora' is wrong. The NP is attributive in both, so dropping the copula is right. But both members are only formation-level in Greek. Ved. svàr is the heteroclite; ἠέλιος is a derivative with no table key. Ved. mahát is the nt-stem mahā́nt-, not *méǵh₂ (whose Vedic match is máhi), so the builder's exact for mahát is a false positive. The engine form méǵh₂ is in neither passage. 'Great sun' is generic (r2 P5). Both daughters have the NP in the accusative (object of ā́ ... apr̥ṇat; Hesiod's accusative catalogue), but the np is NOM.

RV 4.13.3 tám sū́ryam ... spáśam (VedaWeb) and Hymn. Dem. 62 Ἠέλιον ... θεῶν σκοπὸν (glaux; the note's 'not in local corpora' is still wrong). Apposition is what both texts have, so the APPOS conversion is faithful. But both heads are root- or formation-level only. spáś- vs σκοπός, as the note says. Ved. sū́rya- and Gk ἠέλιος are both derivatives, not *sóh₂wl̥, and the builder's 'exact' for sū́rya- is formation-level. Both daughters have the accusative, and both give the watcher a genitive of what is watched (víśvasya jágataḥ / θεῶν ... ἀνδρῶν); the line has neither.

Changed from r2 weak: with the copula gone the line is just the NP, and its head fails. 'Sun', the NP head, is interpolated: RV 1.72.10 diváḥ ... akṣī́ (checked) has no sun word, and the dual means sun and moon. The APPOS head 'eye' is root-level only (ákṣi- vs the diminutive oculus), and the engine's *h₃ókʷs is in neither. The second branch is Macrobius Sat. 1.21.12, quoted from West ('antiquitas' calls the sun Iouis oculus). It is not local, and it is a 5th-c. CE antiquarian report, by all appearances from his chapter of solar syncretism drawn from Greek and Egyptian sources, so it cannot count as an independent Italic witness. Only the genitive *diwés is shared, which is periphery. The Vedic also has the accusative (and, as West quotes it, so does the Latin), not the np's NOM.

Misconstrual: the second branch doesn't carry the phrase. Od. 12.127-128 πολλαὶ ... Ἠελίοιο βόες (AGDT) is a genitive NP 'the Sun's cattle'. RV 7.36.1 ví raśmíbhiḥ sasr̥je sū́ryo gā́ḥ (VedaWeb) has the Sun as subject, releasing the cows (rays or dawns), with no possessive relation, and the note concedes the image differs. What is shared is two common words in different constructions: gʷṓws is exact, while 'sun' is formation-level only (sū́rya- and ἠέλιος are both derivatives). 'Many' is Greek only. The np's genitive structure is Greek only.

*sweh₂dú médʰu (West ch. 2 p. 84; Schmitt §529). RV 1.84.10a-b svādóḥ ... mádhvaḥ (VedaWeb; the two words agree across a pāda break) and Od. 9.162, 17.533 μέθυ ἡδύ, a line-end formula (AGDT), are checked. Both words are exact, and the attribution is attested in both. The OE Finnsburh 39 conjecture is now correctly demoted to support, which fixes r3's finding. The np is right: no daughter has a predication. The NOM is a citation case (Vedic partitive genitive, Greek accusative), honestly marked. The Vedic rests on a single stanza.

As in r3. AVŚ 13.1.24 aśvā ... amṛtāḥ (DCS) and Il. 16.380-381 = 16.866-867 ἵπποι | ἄμβροτοι (AGDT), both checked. Both words are exact. The APPOS conversion matches the texts: amṛ́tāḥ is separated from áśvāḥ by the verb, and ἄμβροτοι is enjambed with a relative clause after it. But the pair is generic (P5): amṛ́ta- / ἄμβροτος go on anything divine, and the scholarly claim (West ch. 3 n. 127) covers only the motif. Minor: the lexicon's oxytone *n̥mr̥tós vs Ved. amŕ̥ta- (accent on the root syllable).

Realized (no built record): h₁nómn̥ moy ḱlutóm. The nominal sentence misconstrues the Greek. In Od. 19.183 ἐμοὶ δ' ὄνομα κλυτὸν Αἴθων (AGDT), κλυτόν is attributive and the predicate is the name Αἴθων, so 'my name is famous' is the plan's sentence, not Homer's. In RV 8.46.14 índram nā́ma śrútyam (VedaWeb), nā́ma is adverbial and śrútyam goes with índram, and śrútya- is a different derivative from κλυτός. Only *h₁nómn̥ is shared, in passages with no common phrase, so r2's reject stands. Converting the clause type does not touch the problem. It also overlaps fame-011 (Od. 19.183).

As in r2. The compound equation *h₁su-ḱléwes- (suśrávas- = εὐκλεής, West ch. 10). RV 1.91.21 and 1.49.2 suśrávasam (VedaWeb) and Od. 21.331 ἐϋκλεῖας (AGDT) are checked. Same prefix, same s-stem, same adjective type; the builder now credits the compound (share 1.0). The np is a good choice. The masculine is interpolated. The NOM is a citation case: all three cells are accusative (the Vedic attributive, the Greek predicative with the infinitive), so ACC would follow the daughters more closely.

Realized (no built record): wékʷesōm tétḱones. The NP 'carpenters of words' stands in no cited text. In Pind. Pyth. 3.113 (glaux) ἐπέων depends on ἐξ and τέκτονες is the subject, with ἅρμοσαν in the relative clause (οἷα σοφοὶ ἅρμοσαν). Nem. 3.4 has τέκτονες κώμων. The Vedic is a simile with another agent noun (táṣṭā iva, RV 3.38.1, 1.61.4), and the Avestan a compound action noun (vacastašti-, N. 5.2, CAB). The head is root-level only. Only *wékʷos is exact, and it is periphery. Dropping the copula doesn't fix that, so r2's reject stands.

Benfey's 'giver of goods', a genuine three-branch formula. Od. 8.325 θεοί, δωτῆρες ἑάων (AGDT), Y. 65.12 aməṣ̌ā̊ spəṇta ... vohunąm dātārō (CAB) and RV 8.51.5 dātā́ vásūnām (VedaWeb) are checked. Vr. 11.12 was not found in CAB; Y. 65.12 suffices. The APPOS follows the Greek and Avestan; 'gods', the NP head, is interpolated (θεοί is not cognate), but the APPOS is itself a secure head-plus-dependent phrase, so the head rule is met. Weak for the form: every cited cell has the suffix-accented agent noun (δωτήρ, Ved. dātā́ with the genitive, Benveniste's type, Av. dātar-), while the engine builds root-accented déh₃tores. That type is attested only in δῶτορ ἐάων, Od. 8.335, which is not cited. The builder's 'exact' for Av. dātar- ignores accent. Fix the lexicon (or cite Od. 8.335) and drop 'gods', and it is sound.

As in r2, with the same unfixed form. The nominal sentence follows RV 1.164.33 dyaúr me pitā́ ... mātā́ pr̥thivī́ (VedaWeb). 'Our' comes from AVP 5.21.1 dyauś ca naḥ pitā pṛthivī ca mātā, which is local (DCS) but not cited in cognate_refs. Outside Vedic only the kin terms are shared. Lucr. 1.250-251 pater aether / matris terrai (LASLA) is a Greek philosophical topos, a derivative witness. Æcerbot (a Christianized charm) is not local, and its folde is root-level. The engine still prints pl̥th₂éwih₂, which Ved. pr̥thivī́ (*pl̥th₂wih₂) contradicts: r1/r2 P6, still open.

The NP head is interpolated and the rest is root-level: the note itself says 'root-level throughout'. *h₂éḱmō 'heaven' is Iranian only. The APPOS head *péyḱos is exact only as the second member of an Avestan bahuvrihi, and there it is attributive to the garment (Yt. 13.3 = CAB YtFra2.3 vaŋhanəm stəhrpaēsaŋhəm), not in apposition to heaven. Vedic has a verb (RV 1.68.10 pipéśa nā́kam stŕ̥bhiḥ), Greek a -μα noun (Eur. Hel. 1096 ἀστέρων ποικίλματα, local in glaux, contrary to the note). The only exact item is the genitive 'stars', which is periphery. No daughter has the line's 'heaven = ornament of the stars' apposition.

Realized (no built record): diwés népoth₁e. The head népōts is Vedic only (RV 1.182.1 diváḥ nápātā, ACC DU, VedaWeb). Hymn. Hom. 33.1 Διὸς κούρους (local in glaux 0013-033, contrary to the note) has a non-cognate head, and Lith. Dievo sūneliai has *deywós. Only the genitive *diwés is shared, so r2's reject stands; the np conversion changes nothing. Both cells are accusative, but the np is NOM. It overlaps divine-twins-001 and bp-east-003 in the genitive.

Down from round 1's sound. The core is real: RV 4.1.10 dyaúḥ pitā́ janitā́ (VedaWeb) against Catull. 64.26-27 Iupiter ipse, ipse ... diuum genitor (LASLA), with Iuppiter containing *dyew + *ph₂tēr and genitor = janitár-. But 'of the gods' is stitched from RV 1.185.6, a different hymn, where devā́nām ... jánitrī are Heaven and Earth (dual, feminine), not Dyaus. The Latin witness is a Hellenistic-modelled epyllion, and diuum genitor probably belongs to the divom pater type that Ennius modelled on Homer. The engine's root-accented ǵénh₁tōr is contradicted by Ved. janitā́ (oxytone) in the cited stanza. The apposition matches all three loci. The builder's exact for janitár- ignores accent.
